content:
The most dangerous product release is the one described as "obvious in retrospect" — before it ships.

---

Paul Graham previewed Replit's next move and used exactly that framing. That's not hype language. That's the specific vocabulary reserved for paradigm shifts.

---

"Vibe coding" was already a wedge. Non-technical founders could suddenly build. But the ceiling was low — demos, MVPs, nothing production-serious.

If Replit removes that ceiling, the entire AI dev tool stack gets repriced.

---

Here's the real threat nobody's naming: it's not to Cursor or Windsurf. It's to the assumption that you need a technical co-founder to go from idea to product.

That assumption is worth billions in consulting, hiring, and agency fees.

---

The builders who win aren't waiting for the release notes. They're already pressure-testing their current stack for the gaps Replit is about to fill.

Identify your weakest workflow assumption now. That's where the disruption lands.

---

Hot take: "vibe coding" was always a placeholder name for something bigger — AI-native product development as a full discipline. Replit is about to make that real.

Agree or disagree?
source_story_title: Replit Poised to Redefine 'Vibe Coding' with Major New Release
source_story_summary: Paul Graham met with Replit CEO Amjad Masad and previewed upcoming features he describes as set to 'redefine vibe coding in a way that will seem obvious in retrospect.' Graham invoked the hallmark of truly big ideas — their inevitable-in-hindsight quality — suggesting this is a meaningful product inflection point for Replit, not incremental improvement.

content:
Most AI startups don't have a strategy. They have a feature that OpenAI hasn't shipped yet.

That's not a business. That's a countdown timer.

---

Paul Graham flagged something rare in a recent YC office hours session: a startup actually built a plan that holds up even if the major model companies commoditize everything around them.

His words: "that's a first."

Let that sink in.

---

The question every AI-layer founder needs to answer isn't "can we grow?"

It's: "does our business still exist in 3 years if Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google decide to own our entire category?"

Most can't answer it honestly.

---

Defensibility in the AI layer doesn't come from the model. It comes from:

→ Proprietary data loops
→ Switching costs baked into workflow
→ Distribution the model companies can't replicate
→ Trust earned in a specific vertical

Build around those. Not around API access.

---

The fact that PG treated this as a milestone tells you everything.

Genuinely model-company-proof strategies are rare — not because they're impossible, but because most founders aren't asking the hard question early enough.

Stress-test your plan now. Not after Series A.

---

Hot take: 90% of AI startups are building on borrowed time and calling it traction.

The ones who survive will be the ones who asked "what if OpenAI ships this tomorrow?" on day one.

Are you building a business or a feature? Be honest.
source_story_title: YC Office Hours Produce AI-Resilient Business Strategy — A First, Per Graham
source_story_summary: In a notable YC office hours session, Paul Graham and a startup team devised a plan specifically designed to remain viable even if major AI model companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) commoditize or capture every adjacent market. Graham flagged this as unprecedented — the first time such a defensible, model-company-proof strategy emerged from an office hours session.
